name: Flanders Red and Oud Bruin
title: Flanders Red Ale: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Flanders red and oud bruin: oak-aged Belgian sour ales with cherry, vinegar and caramel. How they taste, how to serve them and Indian pairings.
tagline: Belgium's wine-like sour: oak, cherry, a sharp edge and caramel underneath. A beer for people who say they hate beer.
tastes:
West Flanders in Belgium is home to red ales aged for a year or two in huge oak vats called foeders. East Flanders gives its cousin, oud bruin, the old brown, usually aged in steel rather than wood and a little sweeter and maltier. Both are blends: brewers mix young and old beer to set the balance of sweet and sour.

A Flanders red smells of black cherry, plum and red currant, with a sharp vinegar note that is part of the style, not a flaw, as long as it stays in proportion. Underneath there is caramel and a little vanilla or oak. Oud bruin swaps some of the sharpness for raisin, fig and toffee. Bitterness is low, because hops would clash with the acid.

The comparison people reach for is red wine, and it is fair: fruity, tart, tannic, food-friendly. The difference is the malt backbone, which gives these beers a sweetness and body no wine has.

profile.look: Deep red to reddish brown for Flanders red, darker brown for oud bruin. Clear. Off-white to tan head with moderate retention.
profile.aroma_flavour: Black cherry, plum and currant, with a sharp acetic edge. Caramel, vanilla and oak behind. Oud bruin is maltier, with raisin and fig. Hops barely noticeable.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium body, moderate to high carbonation. Tart and mouth-watering. Tannic or slightly astringent from oak, finishing dry with lingering acidity.
profile.ingredients: Pilsner or Vienna base, Munich and crystal malts, sometimes maize. Low hops. A mixed culture of ale yeast, Lactobacillus, Pediococcus, Brett and Acetobacter. Long oak or steel ageing, then blending.

in_india: Genuine Flanders red takes a year or more in wood, and few Indian breweries can tie up that much tank and barrel space or risk letting acetic bacteria near their clean beers. Imported bottles turn up in some premium stores in metro cities, with a heavy import duty attached. Because these beers are already acidic and aged, they cope with the Indian cold chain better than most. Serve one with dinner the way you would serve red wine, to someone who thinks they dislike beer.

pairings.why: The beer's cherry and acidity cut the fat, and the dried fruit notes sit well with the fennel and Kashmiri chilli.
Tart beer lifts rich, spiced jackfruit, much as a squeeze of lime would.
Sour cherry with rich duck is a classic match, and the beer cuts the coconut oil and pepper.
Chocolate and cherry meet the beer's own cherry and caramel, and the acidity keeps it lively.

examples_note: We could not verify a Flanders red or oud bruin from an Indian brewery yet. Imported Belgian bottles are your best bet, and a few Indian brewpubs run barrel-aged sours worth asking about.
